The newly emerged altricial nestlings are remarkably small, with a wet weight at birth of just 4.2 grams [Wwb = 4.2 grams], a value that underscores the considerable energy investment required from provisioning adults during the subsequent nestling phase. Females of this species ultimately attain an adult body mass of 79.95 grams [Wwi = 79.95 grams], placing them among the medium-sized members of the Icteridae. This nearly twenty-fold increase in body mass from hatching to adulthood is achieved through a period of rapid mass gain during the nestling stage, a trajectory that is heavily dependent on the consistent delivery of arthropod prey by both parents.

Under the thermal conditions typical of the active metabolic and reproductive period in this species (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), fledging occurs 13 days after hatching [tx = 13 days after hatching]. Achieving this developmental milestone, marked by the capacity for sustained flight and departure from the nest, is a critical juncture in the species' life history. The relatively short fledging period may be an adaptation to reduce the window of vulnerability to nest predators common in the flooded grasslands of its range, such as snakes and small carnivorous mammals, which exert strong selective pressure on nestling development.

Gonadal maturation in the Brown-and-yellow marshbird follows a predictable timeline, with puberty being attained at 39 days after hatching [tp = 39 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This early onset of physiological reproductive capacity, occurring well before the first breeding attempt, is characteristic of many passerines that require additional time to establish territories and secure social standing within their breeding colonies. Field data suggest that the development of the gonads is tightly linked to nutritional condition during the post-fledging period, and individuals that experience poor foraging success may delay the onset of gametogenesis.

The first successful brood is typically produced one year after hatching [tR = one year after hatching], a delay that reflects the seasonal constraints of the temperate austral spring, when insect prey becomes abundant and suitable nesting conditions prevail at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This timing of first reproduction is also evaluated at the species' characteristic high activity temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Females lay between four and five eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between four and five eggs per clutch], and available evidence indicates a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], which yields a maximum reproduction rate of 4 to 5 offspring per year [Ri = 4 to 5 offspring per year]. This modest annual reproductive output is typical of a bird that invests heavily in parental care, with both sexes participating in nest defense and provisioning of the brood over an extended rearing period.

Longevity in the Brown-and-yellow marshbird is estimated at 17 years [am = 17 years], a value derived from mark-recapture studies and consistent with the maximum lifespan recorded for the species under natural conditions at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Such an extended lifespan relative to body size is notable among passerines and suggests a relatively slow life-history pace, where the moderate annual fecundity of 4 to 5 eggs is balanced by a high probability of adult survival across multiple breeding seasons. The species' preference for stable marshland habitats with consistent food resources likely contributes to this pattern, as does its cooperative social system, which buffers individuals against the energetic costs of territory defense and predator vigilance.
